title: Longitude Time Zone Estimator: Solar Time by °
description: Use the Longitude Time Zone Estimator to predict a place's time zone from longitude alone — and see where politics overrules the Sun. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, New York's longitude of 74.0°W divides by 15 to give UTC−5 almost exactly — while Mumbai's 72.9°E suggests UTC+5, and India actually keeps UTC+5:30.
quick_answer: The Longitude Time Zone Estimator predicts a time zone from longitude alone, using the rule that Earth turns 15 degrees per hour. Enter a longitude or a place and read the solar estimate, then see how far real political time zones bend away from it.

body.t: A ship's position, a remote island, a coordinate with no label — longitude alone gives a working time estimate before any database is consulted. For the official answer use the
Spain keeps Central European Time despite sitting on Greenwich longitudes — an estimator makes the political offset visible. Comparing estimate with reality is a civics lesson in disguise.
Every degree of longitude is 4 minutes of solar time. The estimator converts a place's longitude into its mean solar offset — what a perfect sundial culture would keep.

Kathmandu sits at 85.32°E. Divided by 15 that is +5.69 hours — and Nepal actually keeps UTC+5:45, the closest quarter-hour to its solar estimate. The odd offset is astronomy winning, for once.

body.t: China spans about 73°E to 135°E — five solar hours — yet keeps a single UTC+8. In Kashgar the clock says noon when the Sun says it is barely 9 a.m. The estimator shows the gap politics created.

faq: Earth rotates 360° in 24 hours — 15° per hour, 1° per 4 minutes. Dividing longitude by 15 gives the solar offset from UTC; rounding gives the natural zone. Everything after that is politics.
Why do some countries ignore their estimate?
National unity (China's single zone), trade alignment (Spain on CET), and history all bend zones. The estimate shows the Sun's answer; the map of real zones shows governments'.
What about half-hour and quarter-hour zones?

India (+5:30), Iran (+3:30), Newfoundland (−3:30) and Nepal (+5:45) keep fractional offsets — usually because the country's population centres sit between whole-hour meridians, exactly as their estimates suggest.
Does the estimator handle daylight saving?
No — and that is deliberate. It estimates the standard solar-based offset. Daylight saving is a seasonal clock change layered on top, covered by the DST tools elsewhere on this site.
How accurate is it for islands and ships?
At sea, the estimate is close to what mariners historically used — nautical time zones really do follow the 15° rule in 15° bands across the oceans, changing at boundaries the ship chooses.
What is the biggest bend on Earth?
China is the famous one: the far west runs about three hours ahead of its solar estimate. Kiribati's date-line bulge bends the calendar itself — see the International Date Line page.
Can I estimate from coordinates I already have?
Yes — only the longitude is needed. Latitude plays no part in time of day, which surprises people until they picture the planet spinning.
